claims.text: Grain size influences the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in Q235 steel under harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures.
Smaller grain sizes may improve the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
Decreasing grain size increases grain-boundary density.
Changes in grain-boundary density, defect structure, and phase composition associated with smaller grains can improve corrosion resistance.
Annealing time and temperature can be varied to control the grain size of Q235 steel.
Grain size influences the formation and propagation of corrosion pits.
Smaller grain sizes reduce the likelihood of corrosion-pit formation and growth.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, smaller-grained Q235 steel will exhibit lower corrosion-related degradation rates.
The reduced degradation associated with smaller grain size will increase service life.
The hypothesis is intended to apply over a grain-size range of 1–100 μm and from room temperature to 500°C in humid environments containing corrosive species.
Phase composition, defect structure, and processing history may independently influence the corrosion behavior of Q235 steel.
A nonsignificant grain-size–corrosion-resistance correlation or failure of smaller grains to improve corrosion resistance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The study is described as isolating grain size, but annealing time and temperature can also alter defect structure and phase composition, which are explicitly included as mediators or confounders. Without a method to hold these variables constant or quantify and adjust for them, the proposed experiment does not isolate grain size as the governing cause.
